Announcing a New Master of Public Policy and Management
Programme at the Universiti Brunei Darussalam
The Institute of Policy Studies at the Universiti Brunei Darussalam offers a new,
internationally-focused, multidisciplinary Master of Public Policy and Management (MPPM)
Programme, aiming at nurturing excellence in both policy skills and management qualities.
The Programme will be offered in January 2013.
Programme Length: 18 months (1 Year in the Universiti Brunei Darussalam and 1 Semester
in a leading public policy school in the US). The Programme will be delivered by a group of
international and local faculty with expertise in public policy and management.
Programme Benefits:
At the participant level, MPPM will instill policy making, policy management and leadership
skills for current and future civil servants and corporate managers in Brunei and overseas.
Interested students can specialise in energy & environmental policy and management.
Brunei, as a resource rich country in oil, gas and tropical rainforest, can share its unique
experience in policies affecting both energy and forest resources. The Programme will
capitalise on this competitive global advantage of the country.
Financial Assistance: Attractive scholarships are available for qualified students.
Entry Requirements:
Normally an Upper Second Class Bachelor's Degree in a relevant discipline from the
Universiti Brunei Darussalam or a university recognised by the Senate of the UBD. A Lower
Second Class Bachelor's Degree holder with at least 3 years relevant experience will also be
considered for entry. A minimum English qualification of GCE 'O' Level Credit 6 or IELTS
6.0 or TOEFL 550 is required. Also, a minimum Mathematics qualification of GCE 'O' Level
Credit 6 or one "pass" in a subsequent level mathematics subject is essential.
Application closes on 1 September 2012

Why Georgia is different.
Different because we have quadrupled our GDP over the last 10 years and have posted
second quarter 2012 growth in excess of 8% – one of the highest rates globally.
Different because despite global economic challenges we have sustained broad-based
economic growth and maintained a strong momentum of reforms, with an average annual
real growth rate for the latest three years at around 7%.
Different because we have positioned ourselves as the Regional Hub Economy for
businesses – local and foreign alike – wishing to produce and trade in Georgia as well
as from Georgia with the region and the rest of the world.
Different because our credit ratings were upgraded in 2011.
Different because we have a solid sovereign balance sheet, very low levels of debt,
as well as an exceptionally stable and well-managed banking sector.
Different because we are making good progress with the Association Agreement,
free trade and visa liberalization talks with the EU.
Different because we are exploring the possibility of a Free Trade Agreement with
the United States.
Different because ours is one of the lowest tax burdens and one of the friendliest
business and investment environments in the world.
Different because we are one of the safest countries regionally and globally.
Different because we are corruption-free and unequivocally committed to
economic liberty.
Different because we offer exceptional and unique investment opportunities
in many sectors.
Different because we are Georgia.

marked routes and trails, it is no surprise that Taiwan's bicycle
culture has become a traveler's dream. The Taiwan Cycling
Festival in November attracts people from all over the world, all
enthusiastically seeking a journey of discovery.

scene is the perfect respite. The Chihshang Music Festival is an
autumn celebration of the harvest. Enjoy an outdoor meal and
listen to the array of classical music from the various acts. For
a more contemporary music experience, find your way to the
Tiehua Music Village in Taitung to be entertained by both local
and regional bands.
So much of Taiwan is best seen by bike with its abundance of
inspiring and picturesque landscapes, hidden cultural gems and
fascinating historical legacy.

in 1924, it was the longest railway tunnel in Taiwan. Today, it has
been preserved to include a bikeway so visitors can pedal through
for a unique insight into Taiwan's past. Continue to cycle back in
time through the terraced fields, pineapple plants and Madagascar
almond trees of the Longtian bikeway.

A message from
Walter Bagehot
Editor of The Economist
(1861-1877)
You, dear readers of The Economist, know of me. Bankers,
lawyers and academics know of my work. I'm taught to
future kings and queens on how to be a constitutional
monarch. I'm regularly quoted on financial crises, the
monarchy and parliament. Even in outer space, there is an
asteroid named after me! But how many people really
know the real Walter Bagehot? I think I deserve to be
remembered as more than a mere source of soundbites.
Perhaps it was my fault in being too modest - there is only one picture of me, which is used by everyone. Perhaps it is my unusual
surname, which rhymes with 'gadget'. Sadly, I was even rather neglected in my home town of Langport in England's West Country --
just a faded stone plaque on my birthplace, a stained glass window in the church donated by my dear wife, and my gravestone in
the local churchyard.
In 1896 Woodrow Wilson, then a professor at Princeton, made a pilgrimage to Langport, and visited my grave. When people come
to Langport in the future to see where I lived and worked - whether future US presidents or just tourists - I want them to learn
more about me and enjoy a fully rounded Bagehot experience. And I want anyone in the world to have the same access to my work
and legacy
This is what the BAGEHOT MEMORIAL FUND is all about.
Formed in Langport in 2011, the Bagehot Memorial Fund has had Langport's Town Garden named after me, and installed a superbly
illustrated interpretation board; run lots of events and talks, holds an annual public debate during the Langport Festival, and looks
after my gravesite.
They have created a website on all things Bagehot' at www.bagehotlangport.co.uk, a Twitter feed (@bagehotlangport), and a
Facebook page (Bagehot Memorial Fund).
They are building up a unique collection of Bagehot documents and artefacts, based initially on generous bequests from the estate of
the late Lord St John of Fawsley, the recent editor of my Collected Works, and from The Economist.
They have ambitious plans, such as
• making their online resources the 'go-to' places for anything about me or my work;
creating literature and walking trails in Langport about me, my family, my work as a local banker with the legendary Stuckey's
Bank, and my influential writings;
• providing facilities in Langport to make their growing 'Bagehotiana' collection publicly available.
All this needs a lot of money. I should know! Langport is a small, rural community, which takes seriously its role as my home town,
and happily accepts its responsibility to preserve and enhance my legacy. But it needs help. So, please support the work of the
Bagehot Memorial Fund by making a donation or gifting any material, documents, books or artefacts related to me and my work.
Please contact either the Fund's Chair, Barry Winetrobe, on +44 (0)1458 259310 or its administrator, Robin Williams at
Clerk@langport-tc.gov.uk. The Fund operates under the auspices of the Langport Town Trust, a registered charity (#242979) and
has an impressive list of founding supporters. For more information on the Fund, contact Barry or Robin, or look at the Fund
sections of my website, www.bagehotlangport.co.uk, which includes full details on how to make a donation.
Help make my life and work better known by supporting the

Kurdistan Triumph
From Exploration to Production and Export
Forward Looking Policies
When the Kurdistan Region set out to create an oil and industry in the early 2000s, it had a
simple goal: to use the natural resources wisely so that the people of Kurdistan prosper; and
to never again face the terror of genocidal rule.
The Kurdistan Region, which was largely unexplored only ten years ago, has since attracted
the attention of oil and gas companies from more than 17 countries, including the super ma-
jors. With 45 billion of barrels of oil reserves and 3-6 trillion cubic metres of potential gas
resources, it has been identified as one of the few remaining conventional oil and gas frontiers.
In a short time, the region has become one of the most actively explored hydrocarbon regions
of the world.
Now, after several years of exploration and $15 billion dollars of foreign investment, Kurdis-
tan is moving from the development phase to production, export and monetisation of its vast
oil and gas resources. The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) in May this year completed its
first sale of crude oil via a new pipeline to Turkey's port of Ceyan, where it was loaded onto a
tanker bound for Europe. This is the first of many such sales of oil that will be exported through
Kurdistan's newly constructed pipeline.
The KRG's oil policy is fully in line with Iraq's constitution of 2005, and with the goal of help-
ing Iraq to achieve its oil production, export and revenue targets. The export of oil via pipeline
follows a framework agreement made between Erbil and Ankara which adheres to the Iraqi
constitution. Despite differences with the federal government in Baghdad over oil policy, the
KRG remains open to dialogue.
The KRG maintains its goal of producing 1 million barrels per day (bpd) by 2015, and 2 million
bpd by 2019. It is also creating additional export infrastructure to replace the trucking of oil.
As well as completing the pipeline to Ceyhan port with an initial capacity of 350,000 barrels per
day, construction of a second pipeline, with a capacity of 500,000 bpd, could begin this year.
The KRG's vision for its natural resources includes encouraging the development of Kurdis-
tan's large gas reserves and privately run downstream industries. While the vast majority of
gas in Iraq is flared, the KRG has set a rule that natural gas should be processed, not burned.
Last month saw the start of the delivery of natural gas, from the Summail field operated by the
Norwegian company DNO, to fuel Duhok power station. The locally produced natural gas will
displace diesel from the power station, and is part of a KRG strategy to save millions of dollars
every year in costly diesel imports. The plan is to replace diesel with gas in all the Region's
power plants within the next two years. This achievement shows that newly discovered gas can
be monetised in a relatively short time, and is the beginning of the creation of a domestic gas
market.
Now that the Kurdistan Region has moved into the export phase in the development of its oil
and gas sector, other countries can capitalise on its significant energy resources, good security
and stability. After meeting domestic needs, Kurdistan's large reserves of oil and gas can help
Europe and other regions to secure their future energy supplies.

AND A NEW WAY
TO WORK
After a decade of connectivity working styles have
fundamentally changed. "Anywhere" workers divide their
time between traditional corporate offices, home offices
and alternative places such as cafés, public libraries or parks.
They are growing in number. The International Data Corporation
predicts that by 2015 there will be an additional 300 million
workers joining a global workforce of a billion', whilst a 2012 poll
by the Society for Human Resource Management found that
46 per cent of organisations currently use virtual teams,
information adjusts to fit to both screen size and conversation
type. Other smart features include voicemails being read out
on whatever device is being used at the time; the recording
of audio and video conversations search functionality across
multiple channels that include email and Instant Messaging, and
multiple document sources such as data based and document
management systems.
In a connected world, where mobility and collaboration are
the norm, "nomadic" workers expect integration and simplicity
from their enterprise communications solutions. Yet today,
many organisations find themselves operating with fragmented
or incomplete offerings, frustrating users and resulting in
lost business opportunities. Not only are companies dealing
with layers of incompatible technologies - the technologies
themselves are often disconnected from the way business is
actually conducted.
By bringing together voice, video, social media and search
into a smart, seamless, intuitive experience, Project Ansible
has created a frictionless environment that enables
productive conversations and collaboration to take place
across multiple channels.
Unify is aiming to lead from the front with Project Ansible
and drive business process integration. "We are challenging
what businesses should expect of enterprise communications
technology so that we can answer the call of the new way to
work and help enhance our customers' business performance,
said Hamid Akhavan, CEO of Unify,
Poor collaboration is putting distance between employees
and organisations and having an adverse effect on worker
engagement. Dr. Karen Sobel Lojeski, founder of Virtual Distance
International, discovered that teams separated by geography,
operations or affinity suffer a 90 per cent drop in innovation
effectiveness, a more than 80 per cent fall in trust, and a 60
per cent decline in finishing projects on time and on budget.
Lojeski's research highlights the urgent need for organisations
to better understand the challenges of working in virtual
teams, and the importance of effective communication and
collaboration tools, Gallup, a research company, found that
active disengagement costs US companies $450 billion to $550
billion per year.
Given strong interest from customers, partners and carriers, the
market is eager to put the product to the test. "Unify is putting
forth the vision, brand and - with Project Ansible the right
platform, to make it happen, said Zeus Kerravala, principal
analyst at ZK Research, "The Project Ansible user experience is
a great example of how enterprise communication should work
and how we as users want to work. It will redefine how we all
interact, communicate and collaborate."
At Unify we provide a seamless experience in communications
and collaboration designed specifically for the new world of
work, Project Ansible is our newest next generation platform
that aggregates communications from virtually any channel into
a single screen and empowers people to work where, when and
however they wish.
Organisations need to start a new conversation about how to
keep its workers engaged and connected to one another - and
tackle the big question of how to deliver successful pan global
collaboration. At Unity, we believe Project Ansible could provide
the answer

Taiwan, the biker's
paradise
Smooth, open roads. Stunning scenery. English road signs. An ingrained cycling
culture. Stellar road safety.
Unusual for Asia, Taiwan has all the elements of a premier cycling destination.
Moreover, the presence on the island of both tropical and subtropical climatic zones
results in spectacularly varied landscapes. The huge diversity of terrains-including
mountains, valleys, lakes, ocean-offers cycling experiences for everybody.
For experienced cyclists, one popular climb is from Hualien, a coastal city,
to the 3,275m Mount Wuling, in a breathtaking 100km ride from sea level to
mountain top.
For ordinary enthusiasts, there are more manageable rides along Taiwan's
coastal highways. These snake through bustling cities, sleepy hamlets and
gorgeous palm-lined beaches.
Taiwan has also perfected the concept of a Family Cycling Vacation.
Thousands of kilometres of dedicated cycling paths have been built. Parents
easily rent bikes with child seats. One popular family route is the 29km path
around the Sun Moon Lake, Taiwan's largest natural body of water. It features
lush vegetation, ecological diversity, a grand pagoda and Thao aboriginal culture.
Cyclists flock to the Taiwan Cycling Festival, next held from November 8th-
16th 2014, to ride in different events. Competitors race in the gruelling Taiwan
King of the Mountain Challenge (Taiwan KOM) and the Formosa 900, a leisurely
round-island cycle. Meanwhile amateurs opt for the Sun Moon Lake Come!
Bikeday, a 30km event.
This world-renowned festival symbolises Taiwan's commitment to cycling.
The government has invested heavily in the sport. The locals, many of whom
cycle, are always hospitable and helpful. No surprise, then, that Asia's best
cycling experiences are found here.
